content: Lobeline is an alkaloid that is naturally present in several plant species, including Indian tobacco (Lobelia inflata), Devil's tobacco (Lobelia tupa), cardinal flower (Lobelia cardinalis), great lobelia (Lobelia siphilitica), and Hippobroma longiflora. It is also found in Lobelia chinensis. In its pure form, lobeline appears as a white, amorphous powder that is highly soluble in water. Lobeline has been investigated for its potential therapeutic applications, particularly as an aid for smoking cessation. Additionally, it may have utility in the treatment of other substance use disorders, including addiction to amphetamines, cocaine, and alcohol. Pharmacologically, lobeline exhibits multiple mechanisms of action. It functions as a vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) ligand, which can moderately stimulate dopamine release when administered alone. However, it has the ability to attenuate dopamine release induced by methamphetamine. Furthermore, lobeline inhibits the reuptake of dopamine and serotonin, contributing to its neuromodulatory effects. It acts as a mixed agonist-antagonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, binding specifically at the subunit interfaces within the extracellular domain of these receptors. Additionally, lobeline serves as an antagonist at μ-opioid receptors.
